subject: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?

messages.author: 2f40ed71ed2c3b06
messages.subject: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?
parts:
Hello,

  I have a question,

  I fitted a model with indirect effects with "

  theFitMissingBoot <- sem(theModel, data=df, group="PT1", meanstructure = T,
                     missing="fiml", estimator="ML", se="bootstrap")

  " and I got this,

  "

Defined Parameters:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  Z-value  P(>|z|) ci.lower ci.upper   Std.lv  Std.all
    indirect11        0.130    2.315    0.056    0.955   -5.986    3.448    0.130    0.004
    indirect12        8.344    4.384    1.903    0.057    1.100   18.678    8.344    0.680

"

  which seems a little ackward to me,

  because I thought the p-value from bootstrap samples should be lower than 0.05

  if CIs don't contain 0 assuming that the alpha is 0.05.

  Is there anything that I am missing here?

  Sincerely,

 KwH Kim

messages.author: b0660637826aa0a7
messages.subject: Re: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?
parts:
For your indirect2 term:

   Z = Est/SE = 8.344/4.384 = 1.9032847

And the reported p-value is for that Z.

But if you compute CI limits using that SE and critical Z = 1.96, you get something different than the reported CI:

   Lower Limit =  8.344  - 1.96*4.384 =   -.24864
   Upper Limit = 8.344  + 1.96*4.384 = 16.93664

So a CI computed using the same point estimate and SE that are used for the Z-test does include a value of 0, consistent with p > .05. 

What this suggests is that the CI you see in your output was not computed that way.  I don't have time to check the documentation right now, but those limits are the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile points. 

HTH.

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?
parts:
If you're using bootstrapping for inference, the p-value and CIs can disagree. The reason for this is that even when using bootstrapping to generate SEs the Wald statistic and associated p-value assume that the sampling distribution of your parameter is symmetric. However, with a bootstrap sampling distribution there's no guarantee this is the case, and the p value when using a bootstrapped SE isn't terribly informative. On the other hand, with a bootstrap CI, you're just taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (for a 95% CI) from the bootstrap distribution (with some adjustments if you're using BC or BCA confidence intervals) with no assumption about the shape of a distribution. In this case, the CI should give you a more accurate picture of the sampling distribution than the p-value. I tell my students that if they are using bootstrapping to rely on CIs for inference as the p-value can be misleading.

Alex

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?
parts: Well, the p value that is displayed is always based on a Wald statistic (estimate/standard error). the only difference between results using ML to get standard errors and bootstrapping is how the SE is computed. Given that in both cases you're computing the same thing but getting the SE in different ways there's not "p-value from a bootstrapped distribution"

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Discrepancy b2 bootstrap p-value and CIs?
parts:
On 10/07/2016 03:41 AM, Bruce Weaver wrote:
> I wrote: "I don't have time to check the documentation right now, but
> those limits are the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile points." I meant to say
> *I suspect* those limits are the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile points. Alex
> suspects (or knows?) the same thing in his post.

?parameterEstimates

Note that the 'default' value for boot.ci.type is "perc", and level =
0.95. So indeed, the limits are the 2.5% and 97.5% percentile points.

The 'zstat' always is simply the estimate divided by its standard error.

Yves.
